en.question_text: An organization completed its clause 4 context analysis three years ago and has not revisited it. Which statement best describes this situation?

options.text: Non-conformant, but only if a significant security incident has occurred since the original analysis.
Non-conformant, because the management review must consider changes in internal and external issues, and this analysis has never been revisited.
Acceptable, provided the original analysis was approved by senior management and is version-controlled.
Acceptable, because clause 4 is a one-time foundation activity; changes are captured in risk assessments instead.

en.explanation: The organization's situation changes, and an ISMS resting on a stale picture of it stops describing anything real. ISO/IEC 27001 clause 4.1 requires the organization to determine its external and internal issues, and clause 9.3.2 requires the management review to consider changes in those issues. Clause 4.1 imposes no standing monitoring process and no review interval; it is the pairing of the two clauses that makes the determination something the organization returns to. Treating the initial analysis as permanent, or revisiting it only after an incident, leaves the ISMS built on conditions that may no longer hold. Version control and document approval record the analysis rather than showing it is current.

en.question_text: A security analyst logs an asset, threat, and vulnerability in the risk register and selects a treatment for a phishing-related database exposure. What should she do next with the register entry?

options.text: Keep the entry open and review it periodically, updating it if risk status or treatment effectiveness changes.
Archive the entry until the next audit cycle, because the risk register is only updated at scheduled audits.
Close the entry, because selecting a treatment resolves the risk and further tracking is unnecessary.
Transfer ownership to IT, because database risks are technical and IT must maintain all related register entries.

en.explanation: Risk records have to be kept current: an entry that reflects conditions from a year ago no longer supports any conclusion about today's exposure. ISO/IEC 27001 clause 8.2 requires the organization to perform information security risk assessments at planned intervals or when significant changes occur, and clause 8.3 requires the risk treatment plan to be implemented, which is what makes the record something maintained rather than filed. The standard names no 'risk register' and prescribes no format - a register is how most organizations meet the requirement, not a thing the standard asks for. Reviewing entries only at audit time inverts that: the audit tests whether the process ran, it is not the occasion on which it runs.

en.question_text: A colleague claims Annex B of ISO/IEC 42001:2023 is informative, so its guidance can be ignored without consequence for the AIMS. Why is this claim incorrect?

options.text: Annex B is normative and its guidance carries unconditional 'shall' obligations equal in force to clauses 4 to 10.
Annex B is normative and restates each Annex A control verbatim, so ignoring it omits required controls entirely.
Annex B is normative; clause 6.1.3 requires organizations to consider it when defining their risk treatment process.
Annex B is informative but must appear in the Statement of Applicability, requiring written justification for any exclusions.

en.explanation: Annex B is normative, not informative, so the colleague's premise is wrong. Its connection to obligation comes from clause 6.1.3, which requires the organization to define a risk treatment process that considers Annex B guidance for controls already determined to apply — the 'shall' attaches to defining that process, not to each guidance sentence independently. The option stating Annex B restates Annex A verbatim is false; Annex B provides implementation guidance, not a word-for-word copy. The option claiming Annex B guidance must appear in the Statement of Applicability is false; B.1 states organizations are not required to document or justify inclusion or exclusion of implementation guidance there. The option asserting unconditional 'shall' obligations equal to the main body is false; Annex B is written in 'should' and its force is scoped to the consideration required by clause 6.1.3.

en.question_text: A candidate claims: 'Annex B of ISO/IEC 42001 is normative, so its guidance is a hard requirement organizations must implement without tailoring.' Why is this incorrect?

options.text: Annex B is normative but only applies to organizations with AI systems above a defined risk threshold.
Annex B is normative and lists optional controls that supplement Annex A as an extended catalogue.
Annex B is normative and its guidance becomes mandatory only after inclusion in the Statement of Applicability.
Annex B is normative, but it is written in 'should' - clause 6.1.3 e) has the organization consider its guidance when implementing the controls it has determined, not implement every sentence of it.

en.explanation: The candidate's premise is correct and the inference is not. Annex B is normative, but normative STATUS and requirement MODALITY are different properties. Annex B restates each control under a 'Control' heading using 'should'. What gives it force is clause 6.1.3 e): the organization shall define an AI risk treatment process that considers the guidance in Annex B for the implementation of the controls determined under b) and c). So it binds as an input to be considered when implementing those controls, not as text whose own sentences are requirements, and tailoring is expected. The risk-threshold option invents a threshold the standard does not contain. The extended-catalogue option misreads Annex B's purpose: it provides implementation guidance for the Annex A controls rather than additional controls. The Statement of Applicability option is contradicted by B.1, which states that organizations do not have to document or justify the inclusion or exclusion of implementation guidance in the statement of applicability.

en.question_text: An ISMS project manager argues that partial scopes are not permitted and all departments must be included. Which clause 4 concept does this misrepresent?

options.text: The permissibility of a bounded scope: context analysis can justify limiting the ISMS to a subset of the organization.
The requirement that all internal issues be resolved before a partial scope can be formally justified.
The distinction between internal and external issues, which determines whether a department is inside or outside scope.
The requirement to identify all interested parties, which implies all departments are automatically in scope.

en.explanation: A bounded scope is permissible: ISO/IEC 27001 clause 4.3 requires the organization to determine the boundaries and applicability of the ISMS, which is what establishes its scope, and it requires that determination to take account of the issues from 4.1, the requirements from 4.2, and the interfaces and dependencies with activities performed by other organizations. Nothing in the clause obliges the ISMS to cover the whole organization. What it does oblige is that the boundary be deliberate, defensible from context, and available as documented information. Mandating full organizational coverage is a common misconception; so is treating the boundary as an administrative formality rather than a decision the clause requires reasoning behind.

en.question_text: A company completes its clause 4 context analysis at ISMS launch and never revisits it. Why is this non-conformant?

options.text: Context only needs updating when a new legal requirement emerges, since regulations are the sole external issue affecting the ISMS.
An initial context analysis approved by senior management remains valid indefinitely once formally recorded.
The standard mandates a fixed annual review cycle regardless of whether any issues have actually changed.

en.explanation: A change in internal or external issues can alter security objectives and risk exposure, so a context settled once and left behind stops supporting the decisions built on it. ISO/IEC 27001 clause 4.1 requires the organization to determine those issues, and clause 9.3.2 requires the management review to consider changes in them. The standard prescribes no review cycle and imposes no continuous monitoring duty under 4.1 itself, so a fixed annual calendar is a choice rather than a requirement and the trigger is change.
